overview: DISTINCT is a keyword used in the SELECT clause to remove duplicate rows from a result set, returning only unique combinations of the selected columns.
When multiple columns are listed, DISTINCT applies to the entire row (the combination of all selected columns), not to each column independently — a frequent source of confusion.
DISTINCT treats NULLs as equal to one another for deduplication purposes and carries a real performance cost because the engine must sort or hash the result to identify duplicates.
learningObjectives: Use DISTINCT to remove duplicate rows and understand that it operates on the full set of selected columns.
Explain how DISTINCT handles NULLs and compare DISTINCT with GROUP BY for deduplication.
Reason about the performance cost of DISTINCT and when an alternative (GROUP BY, EXISTS, or schema fixes) is preferable.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: DISTINCT is a set quantifier applied to the SELECT list that eliminates duplicate rows from the result, so that each unique combination of the projected column values appears exactly once. It is evaluated after the SELECT projection in the logical query order (after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and SELECT, but before ORDER BY and LIMIT). For deduplication, two rows are considered duplicates when all their projected values are equal, with NULL treated as equal to NULL.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: DISTINCT is like removing duplicate cards from a deck so each unique card appears only once. If you ask for distinct first names, you get the unique names. If you ask for distinct first-and-last name pairs, you get unique pairs — so 'John Smith' and 'John Doe' both stay because the whole pair is what must be unique, not just the first name.
coreConcept.historicalContext: DISTINCT has been part of SQL since its earliest standards (SQL-86), defined as the set quantifier opposite of ALL (which keeps duplicates and is the default). It reflects the relational model's notion that relations are sets of tuples. Historically, engines implemented DISTINCT via sorting; modern engines often use hash-based deduplication. The COUNT(DISTINCT col) form and, later, approximate distinct counting (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, HyperLogLog) were added for analytics at scale.

whyItMatters.business: Accurate unique counts (distinct customers, distinct products sold) underpin core business metrics; misusing DISTINCT can over- or under-count and distort KPIs.
whyItMatters.engineering: DISTINCT is a quick way to dedupe results, but understanding its cost and semantics prevents subtle bugs and slow queries that are hard to diagnose.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because DISTINCT requires a sort or hash over the result, it can dominate query cost on large data; knowing when to dedupe at the source instead is key to scaling.
whyItMatters.cost: On usage-billed engines, the extra sort/hash work and memory for DISTINCT add compute cost; approximate distinct counts can cut this dramatically when exactness is not required.
whyItMatters.reliability: Correct DISTINCT and NULL semantics ensure metrics are stable and reproducible; relying on DISTINCT to mask a join that produces duplicates hides real data-model problems.

coreComponents.name: DISTINCT over a single column
coreComponents.definition: SELECT DISTINCT col returns the unique values of one column.
coreComponents.purpose: To enumerate the distinct set of values present in a column.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Deduplicates by that one column's value, treating NULL as a single value.

coreComponents.name: DISTINCT over multiple columns
coreComponents.definition: SELECT DISTINCT a, b returns unique combinations of the listed columns.
coreComponents.purpose: To find unique tuples, not unique per-column values.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Treats the whole projected row as the unit of uniqueness; identical only if all columns match.
coreComponents.examples: SELECT DISTINCT first_name, last_name FROM customers

coreComponents.name: COUNT(DISTINCT col)
coreComponents.definition: An aggregate that counts the number of unique non-NULL values of a column.
coreComponents.purpose: To measure cardinality, e.g., number of distinct active users.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Counts unique values and, importantly, ignores NULLs (NULLs are not counted).

internalWorking: After the SELECT list is projected, the engine must identify and remove duplicate output rows, which requires comparing rows for equality across all projected columns.
Two common strategies are used: sort-based deduplication (sort the rows, then drop adjacent equal rows) and hash-based deduplication (hash each row and keep one per hash bucket).
For equality comparison, NULL is treated as equal to NULL (unlike in WHERE predicates, where NULL = NULL is unknown), so all-NULL rows collapse into a single row.
The deduplicated set then flows to ORDER BY and LIMIT; if the dataset exceeds memory, the sort/hash may spill to disk, which is the main performance cost.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Projected rows (after SELECT) → DISTINCT sort/hash deduplication → ORDER BY → LIMIT → unique result set
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. After WHERE and SELECT, the engine has projected rows of (first_name, last_name), possibly with duplicates.
2. DISTINCT builds a hash table (or sorts) keyed on the full (first_name, last_name) tuple.
3. As each row arrives, the engine checks whether that exact tuple was already seen.
4. The first occurrence of each unique tuple is kept; subsequent duplicates are discarded.
5. Rows where both columns are NULL collapse to one row, since NULL is treated as equal here; the unique set then passes to ORDER BY/LIMIT.

keyTerminology.meaning: DISTINCT removes duplicates; ALL (the default) keeps them.
keyTerminology.importance: Clarifies that omitting DISTINCT keeps duplicates and that DISTINCT is an explicit, costlier choice.

keyTerminology.meaning: The number of distinct values in a column or expression.
keyTerminology.importance: COUNT(DISTINCT col) measures cardinality, a core analytics metric (e.g., unique users).

keyTerminology.meaning: The physical method (sort-based or hash-based) the engine uses to remove duplicates.
keyTerminology.importance: Determines DISTINCT's performance and memory behavior, including potential disk spills.

importantConcepts.concept: DISTINCT applies to the whole row
importantConcepts.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT a, b is not 'distinct a and distinct b'; it returns unique (a, b) pairs. There is no syntax to make DISTINCT apply to only one of several selected columns (PostgreSQL's DISTINCT ON is a non-standard extension that does this).

For DISTINCT, all NULLs are considered equal, so multiple all-NULL rows collapse into one. However, COUNT(DISTINCT col) ignores NULLs entirely, so NULLs are not counted as a distinct value by that aggregate — a subtle but important asymmetry.

variationsAndTypes: **SELECT DISTINCT col:** Unique values of a single column.
**SELECT DISTINCT a, b, c:** Unique combinations (tuples) of multiple columns.
**COUNT(DISTINCT col):** Count of unique non-NULL values; also AVG/SUM(DISTINCT col) in some engines.

**DISTINCT ON (col) (PostgreSQL extension) and approximate distinct (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT / HyperLogLog):** Engine-specific variants for keeping the first row per key or counting distinct values cheaply at scale.
advantages: **Simple deduplication:** A single keyword removes duplicate rows from results.
**Accurate cardinality:** COUNT(DISTINCT col) gives exact unique counts for metrics.
**Set semantics:** Aligns results with the relational notion of unique tuples.
**Readable intent:** Clearly signals that the result should contain unique rows.
disadvantages: **Performance cost:** Requires a sort or hash over the result, which can be expensive and spill to disk on large data.
**Masks data problems:** Often used to paper over duplicate-producing joins instead of fixing the join or model.
**Whole-row only:** Cannot natively dedupe on a subset of selected columns (without engine extensions).
**Memory pressure:** Building hash tables or sorts for high-cardinality data consumes significant memory.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use DISTINCT when you genuinely need unique rows or exact distinct counts and the result set is reasonably sized, or when a legitimately many-to-many join requires deduplication of the projection.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid DISTINCT as a band-aid for a join that fanned out rows (fix the join), avoid it on huge result sets where approximate counting suffices, and avoid it when a GROUP BY with aggregates expresses the intent more clearly.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: DISTINCT is like collecting business cards at a conference and then keeping only one card per unique person. If you key uniqueness on full name plus company (multiple columns), two people named 'Alex Kim' from different companies both stay. Sorting all the cards to find duplicates takes time — that sorting effort is DISTINCT's performance cost.

commonMisconceptions.myth: SELECT DISTINCT a, b deduplicates each column separately.
commonMisconceptions.reality: DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row, returning unique (a, b) combinations. It never deduplicates one column independently of the others.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DISTINCT is free or always faster than GROUP BY.
commonMisconceptions.reality: DISTINCT requires a sort or hash to find duplicates and is not free. For pure deduplication, DISTINCT and GROUP BY usually produce the same plan and cost; DISTINCT is not inherently faster.

productionConsiderations.scalability: DISTINCT over large or high-cardinality data forces large sorts/hashes that may spill to disk; deduplicating at the source or using approximate distinct counts scales far better.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Using DISTINCT to hide duplicates from a bad join produces brittle queries whose correctness depends on accidental data shapes; fixing the join is more reliable.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: DISTINCT is read-only and retry-safe, but spill-to-disk during deduplication can fail under low disk/memory and should be monitored.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch query plans for hash-aggregate/sort steps introduced by DISTINCT and for disk spills, which signal memory pressure on large dedup operations.
productionConsiderations.security: DISTINCT has no direct security role, but distinct value lists can inadvertently reveal the set of sensitive values (e.g., distinct salaries), so apply access controls.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: On billed engines, prefer APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT for large cardinality estimates and dedupe upstream to reduce the compute DISTINCT consumes.
productionConsiderations.performance: Indexes covering the DISTINCT columns can let the engine deduplicate via an index scan without a separate sort; otherwise expect a sort or hash step.

codeExamples.title: DISTINCT on single vs multiple columns
codeExamples.overview: Contrasts deduplicating one column against deduplicating a multi-column combination to show DISTINCT applies to the whole row.
codeExamples.breakdown: The first query returns each country once. The second returns each unique country-city pair, so the same country appears multiple times with different cities — proving DISTINCT keys on the full row. The third counts unique customer_id values and silently excludes NULL ids.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Query 1: one row per country. Query 2: one row per distinct (country, city) pair. Query 3: a single integer count of unique non-NULL customer_ids.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting query 2 to return one row per country; it returns one row per country-city pair. Forgetting that COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) excludes NULLs can make the count lower than expected.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: An index on (country, city) can let the engine deduplicate via an ordered index scan instead of a separate sort/hash step.

codeExamples.title: DISTINCT vs GROUP BY and NULL handling
codeExamples.overview: Shows that DISTINCT and a GROUP BY with no aggregate are equivalent for deduplication, and demonstrates NULL collapsing.
codeExamples.breakdown: DISTINCT region and GROUP BY region with no aggregate both return unique regions and usually compile to the same execution plan. For DISTINCT, the two NULL rows collapse into one NULL row because NULL is treated as equal to NULL here. COUNT(DISTINCT region), however, ignores NULLs, so it counts only 'East'.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Both dedup queries return 'East' and a single NULL row. COUNT(DISTINCT region) returns 1 because NULLs are not counted by the aggregate.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming the distinct row count equals COUNT(DISTINCT col); they differ when NULLs are present (DISTINCT keeps one NULL row, COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores it).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer GROUP BY when you also need aggregates per group; prefer DISTINCT for pure deduplication. Neither is inherently faster for plain dedup.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A marketing team needs the number of unique customers who placed at least one order last quarter and a clean list of the distinct regions those customers came from, without double-counting customers who ordered multiple times.
endToEndExample.inputData: orders (order_id, customer_id, region, order_date) where a customer can have many orders, producing duplicate customer_id and region values.
endToEndExample.architecture: A relational warehouse query using COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) for the unique count and SELECT DISTINCT region for the region list, filtered by date in WHERE.
processingSteps: 1. FROM orders supplies all order rows.
2. WHERE order_date in the quarter filters rows before deduplication.
3. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) computes the number of unique customers, ignoring any NULL customer_ids.
4. A separate SELECT DISTINCT region produces the unique region list, collapsing duplicate regions (and any NULL regions into one).
endToEndExample.output: An integer count of unique customers and a deduplicated list of regions, accurately reflecting unique entities despite many duplicate orders.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Check the query plan for the hash/sort step DISTINCT introduces and for disk spills on large quarters; validate the unique count against an independent GROUP BY to ensure consistency.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If NULL customer_ids exist, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) excludes them — decide whether that is intended; if a join is added later and inflates rows, do not patch with DISTINCT, fix the join.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Trustworthy unique-customer metrics and a clean region list, with awareness that DISTINCT's deduplication cost is bounded by filtering early with WHERE.

industryUseCases.company: Product analytics teams (e.g., Mixpanel-style event analysis)
industryUseCases.problem: Counting unique active users per day from a high-volume events table.
industryUseCases.solution: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) for exact counts, or APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT/HyperLogLog when billions of events make exact counts too expensive.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate or near-accurate active-user metrics while controlling the heavy compute cost of deduplicating massive event streams.

industryUseCases.company: Data quality / deduplication pipelines (e.g., CRM ingestion)
industryUseCases.problem: Producing a unique list of customer records from sources that emit duplicate rows.
industryUseCases.solution: SELECT DISTINCT over the identifying columns, or GROUP BY with aggregates when a canonical record must be chosen per key.
industryUseCases.benefits: Clean, deduplicated downstream data, with the awareness that recurring duplicates point to upstream model issues to fix.

industryUseCases.company: Reporting teams handling many-to-many joins (e.g., orders to tags)
industryUseCases.problem: A join to a tags table fans out order rows, inflating counts.
industryUseCases.solution: Use DISTINCT to recover unique orders only when the fan-out is legitimate; otherwise restructure with EXISTS or pre-aggregation.
industryUseCases.benefits: Correct counts without double-counting, while flagging cases where DISTINCT is masking a join that should be redesigned.

productionDeepDive.scalability: DISTINCT forces a sort or hash over the projected rows; on high-cardinality or large result sets this becomes the dominant cost and may spill to disk. Deduplicating upstream or estimating with approximate distinct counts scales far better.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: DISTINCT queries are read-only and retry-safe, but large dedup operations that spill to disk can fail under resource pressure; size memory/temp space accordingly.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Heavy DISTINCT analytics should run on read replicas or a warehouse to avoid loading the OLTP primary; results are deterministic given the same snapshot.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: DISTINCT holds no state; reproducibility of distinct counts depends only on the restored data and deterministic projection expressions.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Provide an index covering the DISTINCT columns so the engine can deduplicate via an ordered scan; filter early with WHERE to shrink the set before deduplication; replace DISTINCT-on-join patterns with EXISTS or pre-aggregation to avoid fan-out entirely.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: On billed engines, use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HyperLogLog) for large cardinality estimates to cut compute and memory; dedupe at ingestion so query-time DISTINCT is unnecessary.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: A distinct value list can expose the full set of sensitive values (salaries, diagnoses); apply column-level access controls and masking where appropriate.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track plans for sort/hash-aggregate steps and disk spills attributable to DISTINCT; alert when dedup memory usage or spill volume spikes.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Recurring need for DISTINCT to remove duplicates is a data-quality signal; validate by checking whether duplicates originate from joins (fan-out) or from genuinely duplicate source rows.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log queries whose runtime is dominated by DISTINCT sort/hash steps and alert when distinct counts deviate sharply from historical baselines, indicating data issues.

recommendedPractices: **Use DISTINCT for genuine deduplication only:** Do not use it to mask duplicates produced by an incorrect join.
**Filter before deduplicating:** Apply WHERE early so DISTINCT operates on fewer rows.
**Prefer GROUP BY when you need aggregates:** Use GROUP BY if you also compute per-group metrics.
**Use approximate distinct counts at scale:** Reach for APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT when exactness is not required on huge data.
engineeringStandards: Document why DISTINCT is needed in a query so reviewers can verify it is not hiding a join bug.
Be explicit about NULL expectations: note when COUNT(DISTINCT col) intentionally excludes NULLs.
Prefer EXISTS over SELECT DISTINCT for existence checks to avoid building a deduplicated set.
designRecommendations: Deduplicate at ingestion or via constraints so query-time DISTINCT is rarely required.
Index the columns commonly used in DISTINCT/GROUP BY to enable index-based deduplication.
For 'first row per key' needs, use window functions (ROW_NUMBER) or DISTINCT ON rather than ambiguous DISTINCT.
namingConventions: Alias distinct-count metrics clearly, e.g., COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS unique_users.
Name deduplicated views/CTEs to reflect their uniqueness guarantee (e.g., unique_customers).
documentationStandards: State the uniqueness key explicitly for multi-column DISTINCT (which columns define a unique row).
Document NULL handling decisions, especially the difference between DISTINCT keeping one NULL and COUNT(DISTINCT) ignoring NULLs.
testingStrategies: Test that multi-column DISTINCT returns unique tuples, not unique per-column values, using crafted duplicate data.
Test NULL behavior: verify one NULL row survives DISTINCT and that COUNT(DISTINCT col) excludes NULLs.
Add performance tests to confirm DISTINCT on large inputs uses an index or does not spill unexpectedly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming SELECT DISTINCT a, b deduplicates each column separately.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The syntax reads like 'distinct a, distinct b', so beginners expect independent deduplication.
commonMistakes.impact: Unexpected extra rows: the same a value repeats with different b values, leading to wrong assumptions about uniqueness.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Remember DISTINCT keys on the whole row; to dedupe by one column only, use GROUP BY that column, a window function, or PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using DISTINCT to hide duplicates caused by a fan-out join.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Adding DISTINCT is the quickest way to make inflated counts look correct.
commonMistakes.impact: Masks the real bug, risks subtly wrong aggregates, and adds an expensive dedup step; the query breaks when data shapes change.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Fix the join (use EXISTS, pre-aggregate the child table, or correct the join keys) so duplicates never arise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the count of distinct rows with COUNT(DISTINCT col) when NULLs exist.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Both involve 'distinct', so the asymmetric NULL handling is overlooked.
commonMistakes.impact: Off-by-one or undercounted metrics: DISTINCT keeps one NULL row, but COUNT(DISTINCT col) ignores NULLs entirely.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Decide whether NULL should count; if so, handle it explicitly (e.g., COUNT(DISTINCT COALESCE(col, sentinel)) or add a separate NULL check).

comparisonSection.explanation: For pure deduplication of the listed columns, DISTINCT and GROUP BY (with no aggregate) return the same rows and typically compile to the same plan, so neither is inherently faster. Choose GROUP BY when you also compute per-group aggregates (SUM, COUNT, etc.); choose DISTINCT when you only need unique rows and clarity of intent. GROUP BY also lets you reference the grouped columns in HAVING; DISTINCT does not filter groups.

comparisonSection.feature: Exact vs approximate distinct counting at scale
comparisonSection.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT col) is exact but requires tracking all unique values, which is memory- and compute-heavy on billions of rows. Approximate distinct counting uses sketches (HyperLogLog) to estimate cardinality with small, bounded error in a fraction of the memory and time. Use exact for billing/compliance; use approximate for dashboards and trends where small error is acceptable.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does DISTINCT do, and what does it apply to when multiple columns are selected?
beginnerQuestions.answer: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result so each unique row appears once. With multiple columns, it applies to the entire row — it returns unique combinations of all selected columns, not unique values per column.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress the whole-row semantics; this is the most common DISTINCT misconception interviewers probe.

beginnerQuestions.question: How does DISTINCT handle NULL values?
beginnerQuestions.answer: For DISTINCT, all NULLs are treated as equal, so multiple NULL rows collapse into a single NULL row. Note that COUNT(DISTINCT col) behaves differently: it ignores NULLs and does not count them.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Highlight the asymmetry between DISTINCT keeping one NULL and COUNT(DISTINCT) excluding NULLs.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between DISTINCT and GROUP BY?
intermediateQuestions.answer: For pure deduplication of the selected columns they are equivalent and usually produce the same plan. GROUP BY is the right choice when you also need aggregate functions per group (SUM, COUNT, AVG) and when you want to filter groups with HAVING. DISTINCT only removes duplicate rows and cannot compute per-group aggregates.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that DISTINCT is not faster than GROUP BY for dedup, and that GROUP BY's advantage is aggregation and HAVING.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is DISTINCT considered potentially expensive?
intermediateQuestions.answer: To find duplicates, the engine must sort or hash the projected rows and compare them, which costs CPU and memory and can spill to disk on large or high-cardinality data. Filtering early and indexing the distinct columns can reduce this cost.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Connect the cost to the sort/hash mechanism and mention disk spills and indexing as mitigations.

advancedQuestions.question: When would you replace SELECT DISTINCT with EXISTS, and why?
advancedQuestions.answer: When DISTINCT is used only to dedupe rows produced by joining to a child table for an existence check (e.g., customers who have any order), EXISTS is better: it stops at the first matching child row and returns each parent once without building and deduplicating a large fanned-out set. This avoids the join fan-out and the DISTINCT sort/hash entirely.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show that DISTINCT-on-join is an anti-pattern for existence checks; EXISTS (or a semi-join) is semantically clearer and usually faster.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain how approximate distinct counting works and its trade-offs versus COUNT(DISTINCT).
advancedQuestions.answer: Approximate distinct counting uses probabilistic sketches like HyperLogLog that hash values into registers and estimate cardinality from the distribution of leading zeros, using kilobytes of memory regardless of cardinality. It trades a small, bounded relative error (often ~1-2%) for huge reductions in memory and compute versus COUNT(DISTINCT), which must track every unique value. Use exact counts where correctness is mandatory (billing), approximate where trends suffice (dashboards).
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate awareness of the cardinality-estimation algorithm and the precise/cost trade-off it enables at scale.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A report joins orders to order_tags (a many-to-many table) and then does COUNT(*), producing inflated order counts. A colleague proposes adding DISTINCT. Is that the right fix?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recognize the join fans out each order into multiple rows (one per tag), so COUNT(*) overcounts. DISTINCT on order_id would dedupe but adds cost and only masks the structural issue; the real fix is to avoid counting fanned-out rows.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Prefer COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) if the join must stay, but better is to remove the fan-out: pre-aggregate tags, use EXISTS if tags are only a filter, or count orders before joining. DISTINCT is acceptable only when the many-to-many relationship is genuinely needed in the output.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a daily active users (DAU) and monthly active users (MAU) metric over an events table receiving billions of rows per day.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) per day for exact DAU on partitioned daily tables, filtering by date in WHERE before deduplication. For MAU and rollups over many days, store per-day HyperLogLog sketches and merge them, or use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, so distinct counts compose without rescanning raw events.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Exact COUNT(DISTINCT) is precise but memory/compute heavy and does not compose across days without rescanning. HLL sketches are mergeable and cheap but introduce small bounded error. Choose exact for compliance-grade numbers, sketches for scalable dashboards.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition events by day, precompute and store daily HLL sketches in a rollup table, merge sketches for arbitrary date ranges, and run heavy distinct queries on the warehouse/replicas rather than the ingestion path.

Where does DISTINCT fall in the logical execution order relative to ORDER BY?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows by the full set of selected columns (treating NULL as equal), at the cost of a sort or hash, and is evaluated after SELECT but before ORDER BY.
keyConcepts: DISTINCT applies to the whole projected row, not per column.
NULLs collapse to one row under DISTINCT, but COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores NULLs.
DISTINCT and GROUP BY (no aggregate) are equivalent for dedup and similar in cost.
DISTINCT requires a sort/hash and can spill to disk on large data.
Use EXISTS or pre-aggregation instead of DISTINCT to fix fan-out joins.
commands: SELECT DISTINCT col1, col2 FROM t WHERE cond;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS unique_users FROM events;  -- ignores NULL
interviewPoints: DISTINCT keys on the entire row.
NULL: collapses to one under DISTINCT, ignored by COUNT(DISTINCT).
DISTINCT vs GROUP BY: equivalent for dedup; GROUP BY adds aggregates/HAVING.
Cost is from sort/hash and possible disk spill.
Approximate distinct (HyperLogLog) trades small error for huge savings.
quickNotes: There is no standard way to apply DISTINCT to only one of several selected columns (use DISTINCT ON in PostgreSQL or a window function).
Filter early with WHERE to shrink the set before DISTINCT runs.
Index the DISTINCT columns to enable index-based deduplication.
Prefer EXISTS over SELECT DISTINCT for existence checks.
Recurring DISTINCT often signals duplicates that should be fixed upstream.

keyTakeaways: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows based on the entire set of selected columns, so SELECT DISTINCT a, b returns unique (a, b) combinations, not independently unique columns.
DISTINCT treats all NULLs as equal and collapses them into one row, whereas COUNT(DISTINCT col) ignores NULLs entirely — a subtle but important asymmetry.
DISTINCT and GROUP BY (with no aggregate) are equivalent for pure deduplication and usually share the same plan; choose GROUP BY when you also need per-group aggregates or HAVING.
DISTINCT is not free: it requires a sort or hash that can spill to disk on large/high-cardinality data, so filter early, index the columns, and consider approximate distinct counting at scale.
Using DISTINCT to hide duplicates from a fan-out join is an anti-pattern; fix the join with EXISTS, pre-aggregation, or correct keys instead of masking the problem.
